nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: One of the predictable pronunciations of a phoneme in a particular context. The flap is an allophone of both /t/ and /d/ in American English. allophone allophone

nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: A very quick tap of the tongue tip against the ridge behind the upper teeth, written [ɾ]. In American English /t/ and /d/ are usually pronounced this way between vowels when the second is unstressed: 'water', 'ladder'. flap flap

nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: Between two vowels: the usual environment for flapping. Flapping also follows r, l and n ('hardy', 'party'), so the span grid's [Vɾ] and [VɾV] spans reach back through those to the vowel. intervocalic intervocalic

nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: A context where the difference between two phonemes is lost in pronunciation. Flapping neutralizes /t/ vs /d/ ('writer' and 'rider' can sound alike); Russian word-final devoicing neutralizes voicing (код 'code' and кот 'cat' both end in [t]). Small cues, such as the length of the preceding vowel, may survive. neutralization neutralization

nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: A speech sound as actually produced, described by how it is articulated or how it sounds, whatever word it belongs to. phone phone

nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: An abstract sound category a language uses to tell words apart. English /t/ and /d/ are different phonemes because 'tin' and 'din' are different words. phoneme phoneme

nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: Training a simple classifier (a probe) on a model's frozen internal representations, to test whether some property can be read out of them. probing probing

nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: A model trained on unlabelled audio only, by predicting parts of its own input. No transcripts are used, so anything phonological it encodes was learned from sound alone. self-supervised speech model self-supervised speech model

nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: What is actually pronounced. At every pilot site it is a flap, by construction, so the label can't be read off the sound category. surface form surface form

nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: The phoneme a word has in its stored, dictionary form: /t/ in 'writer', /d/ in 'rider'. The pilot's labels are underlying forms. underlying form underlying form

nodes.label: Finding
nodes.text: Lemma overlap Lemma overlap 25.1% of joint test sites (2,612) have their lemma in training with the same label; the split is disjoint by word form, not lemma. On the 7,586 lemma-unseen sites the gap to MFCC is +0.030, CI [-0.004, +0.073], still short of criterion 1. limitation, registered before the run

nodes.label: Finding
nodes.text: Too little statistical power Too little power The gap to MFCC's paired word-type bootstrap interval is [-0.015, +0.056]: no evidence of an advantage over MFCC, which is not evidence of none. limitation

nodes.label: Finding
nodes.text: Sites aren't what the inventory says Sites mislabelled? A blind listening audit of 80 sites heard a flap in 72 of 74 decidable cases (6 /d/ can't-tells), and the right word and a well-placed clip in all 80. The labels come from the dictionary form and can't be heard under a flap, so the audit clears the sites, not the labels. ruled out for the sites, not the labels

nodes.label: Finding
nodes.text: Too little training data Too little training data? Retraining the single-axis conditions at joint's training size (about 64% of sites) costs 0.006–0.013 at the best layer, against a 0.108 drop from random to joint. ruled out

nodes.label: Finding
nodes.text: Site too narrow (2–4 frames) Sites too narrow? Sites are 2–4 encoder frames wide (median 3, 27.4 ms). For MFCC, whose 25 ms frames see only local audio (deltas reach ±40 ms), a cue outside those frames, such as the preceding vowel's length, is invisible to the probe. WavJEPA encodes the flap ± 200 ms as one excerpt, so at depth its flap frames can carry that context; for WavJEPA the pilot shows only that the cue wasn't linearly recoverable from those frames. Untested: the span grid, registered 2026-10-17, tests both. open

nodes.label: Finding
nodes.text: The cue doesn't generalize to unseen words Doesn't generalize to unseen words The drop from random to joint is mostly the word axis: holding out speakers costs little, holding out word types costs most of the gap above chance. consistent with the result
